parts.text: Luke writes an orderly account to strengthen Theophilus’s certainty about what he has learned. Gabriel tells the elderly priest Zacharias that Elisabeth will bear John, who will prepare people for the Lord in the spirit and power of Elias. Because Zacharias doubts, he cannot speak until the promise is fulfilled. Gabriel then tells Mary that she will conceive Jesus through the Holy Ghost. He will be called the Son of God and reign forever on David’s throne; Mary accepts the message.

Mary visits Elisabeth, who blesses her after the child leaps in her womb. Mary praises God’s mercy, his lifting of the humble, and his faithfulness to Abraham’s descendants. When John is born, Zacharias confirms his name and regains his speech. Filled with the Holy Ghost, he praises God’s promised deliverance and declares that John will prepare the Lord’s way, bringing knowledge of salvation through forgiveness.

chapters.title: The birth and childhood of Jesus

parts.text: A decree from Cesar Augustus brings Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger because there is no room in the inn. An angel announces to shepherds that the Saviour, Christ the Lord, has been born, and a heavenly multitude praises God. The shepherds find the child as described, spread the news, and return praising God. Mary treasures these things in her heart.

Jesus is circumcised and presented at the temple. Simeon recognizes God’s salvation, a light for Gentiles and Israel’s glory, while warning Mary of sorrow and opposition. Anna also gives thanks and speaks of him to those awaiting redemption. At twelve, Jesus remains in Jerusalem among the teachers, astonishing them with his understanding. He tells his parents he must be about his Father’s business, then returns obediently to Nazareth and grows in wisdom and stature.

John preaches a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, fulfilling Esaias’s description of a voice preparing the Lord’s way. He warns that descent from Abraham cannot replace the fruit of repentance. He tells people to share, publicans to take only what is due, and soldiers to avoid violence and false accusations. Denying that he is the Christ, John announces a mightier one who will baptize with the Holy Ghost and fire and separate wheat from chaff. Herod imprisons him for reproving his wrongdoing.

When Jesus is baptized and prays, heaven opens, the Holy Ghost descends in bodily form like a dove, and the Father’s voice declares him his beloved Son. Jesus is about thirty. Luke traces his ancestry, beginning with Joseph as his supposed father, through David and Abraham back to Adam and God.

Full of the Holy Ghost, Jesus endures forty days of temptation in the wilderness. He answers the devil with Scripture, refusing to make bread at his command, worship him for earthly kingdoms, or test God’s protection by jumping from the temple. In Nazareth, Jesus reads Esaias’s announcement of good news and deliverance and declares it fulfilled that day. His hearers turn furious when he recalls God’s help to a widow in Sidon and Naaman the Syrian. They attempt to throw him from a hill, but he passes through them.

In Capernaum, Jesus teaches with authority and commands an unclean spirit to leave a man. He heals Simon’s mother-in-law and many other sick people, silencing devils that identify him as Christ. When the crowds try to keep him there, he explains that he was sent to preach God’s kingdom in other cities too.

chapters.title: Called to follow; authority to forgive

parts.text: After teaching from Simon’s boat, Jesus directs the fishermen to let down their nets. An overwhelming catch makes Simon Peter confess his sinfulness, but Jesus says he will catch people instead. Simon, James, and John leave everything and follow him. Jesus cleanses a leper, sends him to the priest, and withdraws to pray as crowds gather. When a paralysed man is lowered through a roof, Jesus forgives his sins and then heals him, demonstrating the Son of man’s authority to forgive.

Levi leaves the receipt of custom to follow Jesus and hosts a feast. Answering complaints about eating with sinners, Jesus says he came to call sinners to repentance. His disciples need not fast while the bridegroom is present, though they will when he is taken away. He illustrates incompatible combinations with a new garment patch and new wine in old bottles.

Jesus defends his disciples’ gathering grain on the sabbath and declares the Son of man Lord of the sabbath. He heals a man’s withered hand despite opponents looking for an accusation. After a night of prayer, he chooses twelve apostles and heals the crowds. Addressing his disciples, he pronounces blessings on the poor, hungry, sorrowful, and persecuted, and woes on those whose satisfaction and approval are confined to the present.

Jesus commands love for enemies, generosity without expecting repayment, and mercy like the Father’s. He warns against condemning others while ignoring one’s own faults. A teacher cannot lead beyond his own sight, and a person’s words reveal the heart, just as fruit reveals a tree. Calling Jesus Lord must be accompanied by obedience: hearing and doing his words is like building on rock, while hearing without doing leaves a house without a foundation.

A centurion sends messengers asking Jesus to heal his servant, trusting that his word alone is sufficient. Jesus marvels at his faith, and the servant recovers. At Nain, Jesus compassionately raises a widow’s only son. When John sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the expected one, Jesus points to his healings, raising of the dead, and preaching to the poor. He praises John as the promised messenger and exposes a generation that rejects both John’s restraint and Jesus’ eating with sinners.

At Simon the Pharisee’s house, a sinful woman washes Jesus’ feet with tears and anoints them. Jesus tells of two forgiven debtors and contrasts her love with Simon’s lack of hospitality. He declares her many sins forgiven and tells her that her faith has saved her, sending her away in peace.

chapters.title: Hearing the word and trusting Jesus

parts.text: Jesus travels preaching the kingdom, accompanied by the twelve and women who support his ministry. His parable of the sower explains different responses to God’s word: it can be stolen away, abandoned under trial, choked by life’s concerns, or kept with patient fruitfulness. He urges careful hearing and says his family consists of those who hear and do God’s word. On the lake, he stills a dangerous storm and questions his disciples’ faith.

In the Gadarenes, Jesus frees a man from many devils, which enter swine that drown. The frightened people ask Jesus to leave, while the restored man is sent home to tell what God has done. Returning, Jesus heals a woman with twelve years of bleeding as she touches his garment. Though Jairus’s daughter dies before he arrives, Jesus tells him to believe and raises the girl to life.

Jesus sends the twelve to preach and heal, while Herod wonders who he is. He feeds about five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes. Peter identifies him as the Christ of God, and Jesus announces his coming suffering, death, and resurrection. Those who follow him must deny themselves and take up their cross daily. On a mountain, Peter, John, and James see his glory with Moses and Elias, who speak of his coming death at Jerusalem; the heavenly voice commands them to hear him.

Jesus heals a boy his disciples could not help, again foretells his betrayal, and teaches greatness through receiving a child. He forbids stopping someone casting out devils in his name. Setting his course for Jerusalem, he rebukes disciples who want fire called down on an unwelcoming Samaritan village. His answers to prospective followers emphasize the cost, urgency, and undivided commitment of discipleship.

chapters.title: The seventy and the merciful neighbour

parts.text: Jesus sends seventy disciples ahead in pairs to heal and announce God’s kingdom. They must depend on hospitality, offer peace, and warn places that reject their message. He pronounces judgment on cities that have not repented despite mighty works. The seventy return delighted that devils submit to his name, but Jesus tells them to rejoice especially that their names are written in heaven. He thanks the Father for revealing these things to the humble and calls the disciples blessed to see what prophets and kings desired.

A lawyer asks who his neighbour is. Jesus tells of a wounded traveller whom a priest and a Levite pass by, but whom a Samaritan generously cares for. The neighbour is the one who shows mercy, and Jesus commands the lawyer to do likewise. At Martha’s home, Mary listens at Jesus’ feet; Jesus defends her choice when Martha complains about serving alone.

chapters.title: Prayer and the danger of hypocrisy

parts.text: Jesus teaches his disciples to pray for God’s name, kingdom, daily provision, forgiveness, and deliverance. A persistent request to a friend illustrates asking, seeking, and knocking, and Jesus says the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Accused of casting out devils through Beelzebub, he answers that a divided kingdom falls and that his works show God’s kingdom has come. He warns about an unclean spirit’s return and declares those blessed who hear God’s word and keep it.

Jesus refuses the generation’s demand for a sign except the sign of Jonas and contrasts its response with Nineveh and the queen of the south. He urges attention to the light within. At a meal, he denounces Pharisees’ outward cleanliness alongside inward wickedness, neglected justice, and love of honour. He also rebukes lawyers who burden others, approve their fathers’ persecution, and obstruct knowledge. His opponents begin seeking words they can use against him.

Jesus warns against hypocrisy and teaches his disciples to fear God rather than those who can kill only the body. God remembers even sparrows and will provide words through the Holy Ghost when they face authorities. After refusing an inheritance dispute, Jesus warns against covetousness with a rich man who stores abundant goods but dies that night. He tells the disciples to trust their Father’s care, seek God’s kingdom, give to the needy, and store treasure in heaven.

Servants must remain ready for their master’s return, since the Son of man comes at an unexpected hour. Faithful service receives reward; abusive neglect brings judgment, with greater responsibility for those given greater knowledge. Jesus speaks of approaching suffering and division even within households. He challenges people who predict weather but fail to discern their own time, and urges settlement with an adversary before reaching judgment.

Jesus rejects the assumption that people killed by Pilate or a falling tower were worse sinners than others; everyone must repent. A barren fig tree receives another opportunity to bear fruit before being cut down. Jesus heals a woman bent over for eighteen years and exposes the hypocrisy of allowing animals to be watered on the sabbath while objecting to her release from Satan’s bondage. He compares God’s kingdom to a growing mustard seed and leaven spreading through meal.

Travelling toward Jerusalem, Jesus urges entry through the narrow gate before the door closes. Familiarity with him will not excuse wrongdoing, and people from every direction will enter the kingdom while some expecting entry are excluded. He continues his work despite a warning about Herod. Lamenting Jerusalem’s refusal to be gathered, he announces that its house is left desolate. They will not see him until they welcome the one coming in the Lord’s name.

chapters.title: Humility, invitation, and the cost of discipleship

parts.text: At a Pharisee’s meal, Jesus heals a man on the sabbath and challenges objections by recalling how people rescue their own animals. He counsels guests to take humble places and hosts to invite people who cannot repay them. In a parable, invited guests excuse themselves from a great supper because of possessions and marriage. The master brings in the poor and disabled, then sends farther afield to fill his house, excluding those who refused.

Jesus tells the crowds that discipleship requires a claim exceeding family ties and even one’s own life, bearing the cross, and forsaking possessions. As a builder calculates costs and a king considers whether he can fight, a would-be disciple must reckon with these demands. He closes with salt that becomes useless when it loses its savor and calls his hearers to listen.

chapters.title: Joy over the lost being found

parts.text: When Pharisees and scribes complain that Jesus welcomes and eats with sinners, he tells of a shepherd who finds a lost sheep and a woman who finds a lost coin. Each invites others to rejoice. Jesus connects that celebration with heaven’s joy over one sinner who repents.

A younger son takes his inheritance, wastes it abroad, and sinks into hunger. He returns admitting his sin and unworthiness, but his father compassionately embraces him and celebrates his restoration. The older son angrily refuses to join, protesting that his long service never received such a feast. His father assures him that he remains loved and shares everything, yet explains that celebration is fitting because his brother, who was dead and lost, is alive and found.

An unjust steward facing dismissal reduces his master’s debtors’ bills to secure their future welcome; his master commends his shrewdness. Jesus teaches the responsible use of earthly wealth, faithfulness in small matters, and the impossibility of serving both God and mammon. Covetous Pharisees ridicule him, but he says God knows their hearts. He affirms the enduring force of God’s law and speaks against divorce followed by remarriage.

Jesus tells of a rich man living luxuriously while the suffering Lazarus lies at his gate. After death, Lazarus is comforted with Abraham while the rich man suffers torment, separated by an impassable gulf. The rich man asks for Lazarus to warn his brothers. Abraham answers that they have Moses and the prophets; if they refuse that testimony, even someone rising from the dead will not persuade them.

chapters.title: Faithful service and the Son of man’s day

parts.text: Jesus warns against causing others to stumble and commands repeated forgiveness when a brother repents. He speaks of faith as a mustard seed and teaches that servants who obey have only done their duty. Ten lepers ask for mercy and are cleansed while going to show themselves to the priests. Only one, a Samaritan, returns to glorify God and thank Jesus; Jesus commends his faith.

Questioned about God’s kingdom, Jesus says it does not come with outward observation and is within them. He warns his disciples against false reports about the Son of man, whose day will be unmistakable like lightning, though suffering and rejection must come first. As in Noe’s and Lot’s days, ordinary life will precede sudden destruction. He warns against turning back, describes people taken and left, and answers with an image of eagles gathering where the body is.

Jesus tells of a widow whose persistence moves an unjust judge, encouraging continual prayer and trust that God will vindicate his elect. He asks whether the Son of man will find faith when he comes. Another parable contrasts a Pharisee boasting of his righteousness with a publican pleading for mercy; the humbled sinner goes home justified. Jesus welcomes little children and says God’s kingdom must be received like a child.

A rich ruler becomes sorrowful when Jesus tells him to distribute his wealth and follow him. Jesus explains the difficulty riches pose, yet what is impossible for people is possible with God, and sacrifices for the kingdom receive reward. He foretells his mistreatment, death, and resurrection at Jerusalem, but the twelve do not understand. Near Jericho, a blind beggar persistently calls him Son of David and receives his sight, following him and praising God.

In Jericho, Jesus calls Zaccheus down from a tree and stays at his house. Zaccheus promises generosity and restitution, and Jesus declares that salvation has come, explaining his mission to seek and save the lost. Because people expect God’s kingdom immediately, he tells of a nobleman who travels to receive a kingdom and returns to assess his servants. Faithful trading receives authority, an unproductive servant loses his money, and rebellious citizens face judgment.

Jesus rides toward Jerusalem on a colt as his disciples praise God and welcome the king coming in the Lord’s name. He refuses to silence them, yet weeps over the city because it has not recognized its visitation and will suffer destruction. He drives buyers and sellers from the temple, declaring it a house of prayer rather than a den of thieves. Leaders seek his death, but the people eagerly hear him.

Religious leaders challenge Jesus’ authority, but decline to answer his question about John’s baptism, so he does not answer theirs. He tells of tenants who abuse a vineyard owner’s servants and kill his beloved son; the owner destroys them and gives the vineyard to others. The leaders recognize the parable concerns them. Spies then try to trap Jesus over tribute to Cesar, but he tells them to render Cesar’s things to Cesar and God’s things to God.

Sadducees question resurrection through a woman successively married to seven brothers. Jesus explains that those attaining the resurrection neither marry nor die and cites God’s continuing relationship with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He asks how Christ can be David’s son when David calls him Lord. Finally, he warns against scribes who seek honour, exploit widows, and disguise their conduct with long prayers.

Jesus values a poor widow’s two mites above the gifts of the rich because she gives her whole livelihood. He predicts the temple’s destruction and warns against false claimants, panic over wars, and assuming the end is immediate. Nations will fight and disasters will occur, but first his followers will face persecution, betrayal, and even death. Such trials provide opportunities to testify, and he promises wisdom their opponents cannot resist.

When Jerusalem is surrounded by armies, people in Judea must flee. The city faces desolation, captivity, and Gentile domination until their times are fulfilled. Signs in heaven and distress on earth precede the Son of man’s glorious coming. As budding trees announce summer, these signs announce God’s kingdom. Jesus affirms his words’ certainty and commands watchfulness and prayer, lest indulgence and everyday cares leave his hearers unprepared.

Judas agrees to betray Jesus for money. Peter and John prepare the passover, where Jesus gives bread as his body and the cup as the new testament in his blood, to be remembered by his followers. He announces betrayal, answers the disciples’ dispute about greatness by pointing to service, and promises them a place in his kingdom. He warns Peter that Satan seeks to sift them and predicts his three denials, while assuring him of prayer and future responsibility to strengthen others.

On the Mount of Olives, Jesus submits to the Father’s will in agonized prayer while the disciples sleep. Judas leads the arresting crowd; Jesus heals the ear cut off by a follower and submits to arrest. Peter denies knowing him three times, then weeps when Jesus looks at him. After mocking and beating, the council questions Jesus, who speaks of the Son of man seated at God’s right hand.

Jesus is accused before Pilate, who finds no fault in him and sends him to Herod. Herod mocks him and returns him, and Pilate again declares that he has done nothing deserving death. The crowd insists on crucifixion and demands Barabbas, imprisoned for rebellion and murder. Pilate finally grants their demand and hands Jesus over.

Simon of Cyrene carries the cross, and Jesus warns mourning women of coming distress. At Calvary he is crucified between two criminals, asks the Father to forgive his executioners, and endures mockery. One criminal acknowledges Jesus’ innocence and asks to be remembered; Jesus promises him paradise that day. Darkness falls, the temple veil tears, and Jesus commits his spirit to the Father. A centurion declares him righteous. Joseph of Arimathea buries him, while women observe the tomb, prepare spices, and rest on the sabbath.

chapters.title: The risen Christ opens the Scriptures

parts.text: Women find the tomb empty and hear from two men in shining garments that Jesus has risen as he foretold. Their report is disbelieved, though Peter visits and wonders. On the road to Emmaus, Jesus joins two discouraged followers without being recognized and explains from Moses and the prophets why Christ must suffer and enter glory. They recognize him when he breaks bread, and he vanishes. They return to Jerusalem, where others report his appearance to Simon.

Jesus appears among the gathered disciples, shows his hands and feet, and eats before them to demonstrate that he is not merely a spirit. He opens their understanding of the Scriptures concerning his death, resurrection, and the preaching of repentance and forgiveness to all nations. They must wait in Jerusalem for power from above. Near Bethany, he blesses them and is carried into heaven; they return worshipping and rejoicing.
